opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea is that the local learning coefficient, the LLC, is a measure of model complexity. It tells you something like how many effective degrees of freedom the model is using near a particular solution. In its original form it's a global quantity: you compute it for the whole network at once. The refined variants come from noticing that you can restrict that measurement in two different ways.

The first is the weight-refined LLC. Instead of letting all the parameters vary when you estimate the LLC, you only let a subset vary, say the weights belonging to a single attention head, and freeze everything else. That gives you a complexity measure for that component specifically. The second is the data-refined LLC, where you change the data distribution you measure against. You might compute the LLC with respect to code, or natural-language text, or some synthetic distribution, instead of the full training distribution.

What gets interesting is combining the two. In the work we did on a small two-layer attention-only language model, we tracked these per-head LLCs over the course of training. The heads separate into groups based on how their LLC curves evolve. Some heads have curves with a characteristic bump or plateau at the point where induction circuits form, and those turn out to be the induction heads and the previous-token heads that feed into them. Other heads have different signatures, and those correspond to different roles, like heads specializing in particular kinds of tokens or positional patterns.

So the weight-refined LLC acts as a kind of developmental fingerprint. Without looking at attention patterns or doing any circuit analysis, you can cluster heads by how their complexity changes over training, and those clusters line up quite well with the functional categories you'd find through more traditional interpretability.

Then the data-refined version lets you ask what a given head is specialized for. If a head's LLC is much higher when you measure it on, say, code than on general text, that tells you the head is doing a lot of its work on that distribution. We found heads that seemed specialized in this way, including one that looked like it was handling something like nested brackets or structured syntax, and that was not obvious beforehand. The refined LLC pointed us to it, and then we could verify it with more conventional methods.

The bigger-picture point is that this gives you a principled, theoretically grounded tool for localizing structure, both in where it lives in the network and in what data it's responsive to. It also gives you that across training time, not just at the end. That's part of the broader developmental interpretability agenda: we think that understanding how structure forms is a really useful lens on what the final structure is.

r001.rationale: It explains that data-refined LLC changes the data distribution used for measurement, such as measuring on code or natural-language text.

r002.rationale: It says to vary only a component’s weights, such as one attention head’s, while freezing everything else, yielding a component-specific complexity measure.

r003.rationale: It says per-head LLC curves were tracked during training and that heads can be clustered by how those curves evolve.

r004.rationale: It explains that measuring a head’s LLC on different distributions can show what it specializes in.

r005.rationale: It mentions code evaluation and an induction-circuit training signature, but does not say code evaluation distinguishes induction heads whose LLC signatures previously appeared similar.

r006.rationale: It mentions a head associated with nested brackets or structured syntax, but does not identify it as an induction head distinguished by code evaluation or say it specializes in syntax tokens.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea here is that the LLC, the local learning coefficient, is a measure of how degenerate the loss landscape is around a particular point in weight space. It's telling you something about how many directions you can move in without changing the loss, roughly how "complex" the model is at that point. The normal version measures that for the whole network, with respect to the full training distribution.

The refined LLC is what you get when you relax both of those things. You can restrict which weights you're looking at, and you can restrict which data you're evaluating the loss on. So instead of asking "how complex is this network," you can ask "how complex is this attention head, with respect to this particular subset of data." You hold everything else fixed, you perturb only the weights of that head, and you look at how the loss on, say, code tokens or bracket-matching tokens responds to those perturbations.

Once you can do that, you get a kind of fingerprint for each head. You take a bunch of different data subsets, compute the refined LLC for each head on each subset, and you can see which heads are "complex" with respect to which kinds of data. A head that's doing something very specific, like an induction-type behavior, will show a lot of structure on data where induction matters and look basically flat elsewhere. Heads that are doing something more generic will look much more uniform.

The nice thing is that this is a pretty agnostic way to find specialization. We didn't have to go in with a hypothesis about what each head was doing. We just clustered the heads based on their refined LLC profiles across data subsets, and the clusters that came out lined up quite well with the things people had already found through more hands-on mechanistic interpretability, previous-token heads, induction heads, heads that activate on particular kinds of syntax. And in a couple of cases it surfaced heads with weird profiles that we hadn't been looking for, which then turned out to have interpretable behavior when we went and looked.

So I'd frame it as a developmental and structural tool rather than a circuit-finding tool. It won't tell you the exact algorithm a head is implementing, but it tells you where to look, and it gives you a principled quantity you can track over training to see when that specialization emerges.

r001.rationale: The response says the refined LLC can restrict the data used to evaluate loss, such as using particular token subsets.

r002.rationale: It says to hold everything else fixed and perturb only the weights of the attention head, measuring that head's complexity.

r003.rationale: It describes clustering heads by refined LLC profiles across data subsets, but does not state that heads in two-layer Transformers are clustered by learning-coefficient trajectories during training.

r004.rationale: It explains that comparing refined LLC profiles across data subsets reveals which kinds of data a head is specialized for.

r005.rationale: The response mentions induction-type behavior and code tokens as examples, but does not say code evaluation distinguishes induction heads whose signatures previously appeared similar.

r006.rationale: It mentions heads associated with syntax generally, but does not identify a distinguished induction head as apparently specialized to syntax tokens.

astra-6.text:
The idea is to take the local learning coefficient, which is normally a measure of the geometry of the loss landscape around a solution, and refine what you’re looking at. You can ask about a particular subset of the parameters—say, the parameters belonging to one attention head—and you can also change the distribution of inputs on which you evaluate the loss.

So, for a particular head, we allow its parameters to fluctuate while keeping the rest of the model fixed, and ask how constrained those fluctuations are by the loss. Roughly speaking, the coefficient measures an effective number of directions in which perturbing that head changes the model’s behavior. It’s not just counting parameters, and it’s not directly measuring how important the head is.

Then you can track that quantity over training and compare heads. Heads with similar trajectories become candidates for having similar roles, and changes in those trajectories can indicate that something is happening in their development. Refining the input distribution gives you another way to probe that: does this head look different when we evaluate it on one kind of data versus another?

That gives us a way to look for structure and specialization without first having to specify exactly what every head does. But you still want to connect those measurements to behavioral experiments or other interpretability tools. The coefficient gives you a clue about the structure; it doesn’t, by itself, tell you that a head implements a particular algorithm.

r001.rationale: It says the input distribution used to evaluate the loss can be changed to refine the measurement.

r002.rationale: It describes varying one head’s parameters while keeping the rest of the model fixed, then measuring how constrained those variations are by the loss.

r003.rationale: It says heads with similar trajectories may have similar roles, but does not state that heads in studied two-layer Transformers can be clustered by their trajectories.

r004.rationale: It describes comparing a head’s measurement across data types as a way to probe specialization.

r005.rationale: It does not mention code evaluation or induction heads with previously similar signatures.

r006.rationale: It does not identify an induction head as specialized to syntax tokens.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea is to take the local learning coefficient, which gives you a notion of the effective complexity of a solution, and refine it by asking which parameters and which data you’re looking at. Rather than getting one number for the whole model, you can ask about an individual attention head, or about that head’s behavior on a particular distribution of inputs.

Concretely, you let the parameters of that head vary while holding the rest of the model fixed, and look at how the loss changes in its neighborhood. The refined LLC characterizes the geometry of that loss landscape. It’s sensitive to how many directions the head is constrained in, rather than just how many parameters it has.

Then you can track those measurements over training and compare heads. Heads can develop different complexity profiles, and changes in those profiles can help you identify when they begin to specialize. Refining the data distribution gives you another handle: does a head’s complexity look different when you evaluate it on examples that require a particular behavior?

I’d emphasize that the coefficient doesn’t, by itself, tell you, ‘This is an induction head.’ You still need to inspect the behavior and do interventions to establish that. But it gives you a way to find potentially meaningful distinctions between heads and transitions during training, without having to specify every possible function in advance.

r001.rationale: It says the data distribution can be refined by evaluating a head on particular input distributions.

r002.rationale: It describes varying one head’s parameters while holding the rest of the model fixed, then measuring the loss landscape around that head.

r003.rationale: It says to compare heads and track measurements over training, but does not state that heads in studied two-layer Transformers can be clustered by their learning-coefficient trajectories.

r004.rationale: It explains that comparing a head’s complexity across behavior-specific input distributions can help identify its specialization.

r005.rationale: It does not mention code evaluation or induction heads with previously similar signatures.

r006.rationale: It does not identify an induction head as specialized to syntax tokens.
